Recall what happens when two heterozygous F1 flies (GgRr x GgRr) assort independently - think of the classic F2 dihybrid phenotype pattern with two dominant traits.
walkthrough:
Linking Counted Offspring To A Statistical Test**
When you count different phenotype classes, you need a way to decide if any difference from prediction is just chance or really significant. The chi-squared test does exactly that by comparing observed numbers with expected numbers.

Remembering The Standard Dihybrid Expectation**
Both original parents are homozygous, so F1 are all GgRr grey body red eyes. Intercrossing F1, if the two autosomal genes assort independently, gametes combine at random to give four phenotypes in the familiar 9 grey-red : 3 grey-brown : 3 black-red : 1 black-brown ratio.
Final answer: statistical test: chi-squared ($\chi^2$) test; expected F2 phenotypic ratio: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

walkthrough:
Setting Up The Parental Genotypes**
A test cross means crossing the fly you want to test with a homozygous recessive fly. Here that is GgRr (heterozygous grey body red eyes) x ggrr (black body brown eyes). Only ggrr guarantees every allele from the tested fly is visible in the offspring.

Writing The Gametes**
The GgRr parent can make four gamete types: $GR$, $Gr$, $gR$, $gr$. The ggrr parent can make only $gr$. This is the key to seeing all possibilities in one cross.

Combining To Get Offspring**
Joining $gr$ to each of the four gives: $GgRr$, $Ggrr$, $ggRr$, $ggrr$ in equal expectation. Lay this out clearly as parental genotypes, gametes in circles, then a Punnett square or lines to offspring.

Adding The Phenotypes**
Because G is dominant for grey and R is dominant for red: GgRr = grey body red eyes, Ggrr = grey body brown eyes, ggRr = black body red eyes, ggrr = black body brown eyes. Four genotypes give four phenotypes.

Final answer: parents: GgRr x ggrr; gametes: GR, Gr, gR, gr x gr; offspring genotypes: GgRr, Ggrr, ggRr, ggrr; offspring phenotypes: grey body red eyes, grey body brown eyes, black body red eyes, black body brown eyes.

walkthrough:
Describing The Observed Numbers**
If assortment were independent, the test cross should give about 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, roughly 67 of each class from 268 total. Instead you see 123 grey-red and 132 black-brown but only 7 grey-brown and 6 black-red. So two classes are in huge majority.

Spotting Parental Types**
The majority classes, grey body red eyes and black body brown eyes, look exactly like the original homozygous parents (GGRR and ggrr) and the F1 combination. That tells you these are parental phenotypes, while the two tiny classes are new recombinant phenotypes.

Explaining With Linkage**
This pattern means the two loci are on the same chromosome, they are linked. In the F1 heterozygote, G is on the same chromosome as R, and g is on the same chromosome as r. During meiosis the whole chromosome tends to be passed on together, so there is no independent assortment.

Accounting For The Few Recombinants**
The 7 + 6 recombinant flies arise when crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I swaps segments, creating new Gr and gR chromatids. Because crossing over between these two loci is rare, recombinants are few.

Interpreting Gene Distance**
A very low proportion of recombinants, about 13 out of 268 or ~4.9%, shows the two genes are close together on the chromosome. The closer linked genes are, the less likely crossing over occurs between them.

Final answer: Description: not 1:1:1:1, most offspring are grey body red eyes (123) and black body brown eyes (132), very few are grey body brown eyes (7) and black body red eyes (6). Explanation: genes for body and eye colour are linked on the same autosome, G linked to R and g linked to r, so no independent assortment; parental combinations predominate; rare recombinants formed by crossing over; low recombinant frequency indicates genes are close together.
